note: Ulysses, who has finished the story of his last voyage (Canto 26). In Dante's Italian it is this flame that leaves with Virgil's permission. The poets stay where they are, on the bridge.

A hollow bull of brass made by the craftsman Perillus for Phalaris, tyrant of Agrigento in Sicily in the 6th century BC. Victims were roasted inside, and their screams came out sounding like a bull's bellow. Phalaris tried it first on its maker. Dante calls that justice.
The soul's words have no mouth to leave by. At first they come out as the roar of fire, until they work up to the tip and make it move like a tongue.

quote: who just now spoke in Lombard dialect
context: Virgil came from Mantua, in Lombardy. The soul has overheard him sending Ulysses away and caught the accent of northern Italy, a surprising detail for an ancient Roman addressing a Greek.

quote: 'Go now, I urge you no further'
note: Virgil's words of dismissal to Ulysses. In the Italian they begin with istra, a Lombard word for "now".

context: The soul's home ground, where he fought most of his wars. His first thought is for news of it.
The hill country of Montefeltro. The speaker is never named in the canto, but his birthplace and his story identify him.

note: Virgil spoke to the Greeks himself. With an Italian, and a modern one, Dante can do the talking.
The lords who had taken over the once self-governing cities of Romagna. Dante goes through them city by city, naming each lord by the animal on his coat of arms.

The da Polenta family, lords of Ravenna since 1275, whose arms showed an eagle. Guido da Polenta the elder was the father of Francesca da Rimini (Inferno 5). Dante spent his last years in Ravenna as the guest of this family, and died there in 1321.
A small town on the coast south of Ravenna, valuable for its salt works.

quote: The city that once made the long resistance
note: Forlì. It held out against an army of French and Italian troops sent by Pope Martin IV, and in 1282 the defenders slaughtered the attackers. The commander of the defense was Guido da Montefeltro himself: Dante is telling the soul about his own greatest victory.
The Ordelaffi family, lords of Forlì, whose arms showed a green lion.

quote: The old Mastiff of Verrucchio and the young one
note: Malatesta da Verrucchio, lord of Rimini, and his son Malatestino. Two other sons of the old Mastiff were Gianciotto and Paolo, the husband and the lover of Francesca da Rimini (Inferno 5).
Montagna de' Parcitati, leader of the Ghibellines of Rimini. The Malatesta captured him in 1295, and Malatestino had him killed in prison.

quote: The cities along the Lamone and Santerno rivers
note: Faenza, on the Lamone, and Imola, near the Santerno.

quote: the little Lion of the white den
note: Maghinardo Pagani, whose arms were a blue lion on a white field. He was a Ghibelline in Romagna and fought for the Guelphs in Tuscany, which is the changing of sides in the next line.

quote: the city whose flank the Savio bathes
note: Cesena. Alone among these cities it had no outright lord and still governed itself in part, though powerful men led it.
The usual offer to the damned: fame among the living in return for their story. To this soul it is a threat, as his answer shows.

quote: If I believed my answer were being given
note: He speaks only because he is sure the story can never get out. He is wrong: Dante is alive and will write it down. The master deceiver is deceived again. T. S. Eliot set these lines, in Italian, at the head of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock.
Guido joined the order in 1296, in his seventies, and died two years later.
The knotted rope that Franciscans wear as a belt, a sign of their vow of poverty.

context: The pope is never named in the canto. Guido curses him as the man who pulled him back into sin after he had made his peace with God.

quote: not those of a lion, but of a fox
note: Force and fraud, the two ways of doing wrong. The pairing of lion and fox comes from Cicero's On Duties, which calls fraud the more hateful of the two. Hell is built on the same ranking: the fraudulent lie below the violent.

Old age as a ship coming into harbor. Dante had used the same image in his earlier book the Convivio, and there held up Guido by name as a noble man who lowered his sails in time. This canto takes the praise back.

quote: the Leader of the modern Pharisees
note: Boniface again. The Pharisees of the Gospels were religious leaders whom Christ attacked as hypocrites. Their modern heirs, for Dante, are the corrupt clergy of the papal court.
The Lateran was the pope's palace in Rome. The war, begun in 1297, was against the Colonna, a great Roman family. Its two cardinals had declared Boniface's election invalid.

The last Christian city in the Holy Land, which fell to the sultan of Egypt in 1291. The pope's enemies were not Muslims who had taken it, nor Christian merchants who broke the Church's ban on trading with them. A pope with a holy war waiting made war on his own neighbors.

quote: used to make its wearers lean
note: A dig at the Franciscans of Dante's day, who no longer fasted as the first friars had.

context: In the legend, Constantine was a pagan struck with leprosy. He sent for Pope Sylvester, who was hiding from persecution in a cave on Mount Soracte, north of Rome. Sylvester baptized him and he was healed. Boniface sends for a holy man too, but to feed his sickness, not cure it.

note: The pope forgives the sin before it is committed. This is the trick the whole canto turns on, and the devil will take it apart.
The Colonna stronghold in the hills east of Rome, the ancient Praeneste. It could not be taken by force. In 1298 the Colonna surrendered it on a promise of pardon, and Boniface had it torn down.
The keys of the kingdom of heaven, which Christ gave to Peter with the power to bind and loose (Matthew 16:19). Popes claimed them as Peter's successors.

Celestine V, the hermit pope who resigned in 1294 after five months, giving up the keys. Boniface, who was said to have talked him into it, sneers at him. Celestine is usually taken to be the one "who made the great refusal" in Inferno 3.

quote: a long promise with short fulfillment
note: Promise much and deliver little: offer the Colonna full pardon, then break your word once they open the gates.

context: He comes to collect the soul of a friar of his order, and loses it to a devil.

note: A fallen angel of the order of Cherubim, the second highest, whose special gift was knowledge. It suits a devil who argues like a scholar.

The scene has a mirror in Purgatorio 5. There Guido's son Buonconte, a soldier who died unconfessed, is saved by a single tear of repentance at the last moment, and it is the angel who carries him off while the devil protests.

quote: one who doesn't repent cannot be absolved
note: The devil's proof. Forgiveness needs repentance, and repentance means turning away from the sin. No one can be sorry for a sin while still meaning to commit it, so the pope's absolution was worth nothing. Guido, the cleverest man of his time, let himself be fooled by a bad argument.

context: Eight coils of the tail send Guido to the eighth circle. Minos adds the ditch in words, and bites his own tail in fury at the sinner.

note: The fire that steals its sinner from sight, as Canto 26 put it: each flame hides a soul like stolen goods.
The ninth ditch, where those who split apart families, cities and faiths are themselves cut open. It is the subject of Canto 28.
